draft.title: Limits of epidemiology
card: Epidemiology counts and compares health data, such as rates of illness or death. These numbers show what is happening in a population.
The numbers do not explain why a pattern exists. A higher rate of a disease in one group shows a difference, but not what caused it.
Statistics do not show how people feel about their own health. Two people with the same illness may report very different wellbeing.
Data can show that one group has worse health than another. It does not by itself explain the social or economic causes behind that gap, so other kinds of research are also needed.
draft.remember: Epidemiology shows what is happening, and other research is needed to learn why.

a.q: A report shows that diabetes rates are higher in one region than in another. What does the report not tell us on its own?
opts: Why the rates differ between the regions
Which region has the higher rate
How many people have diabetes in each region
Whether the rates differ between the regions
a.why: Rates show that a difference exists and how big it is. They do not explain what causes it. The other options are all things the numbers do show, so the tempting choice about which region is higher is wrong.
a.clue: Counting a difference is not the same as explaining it.

b.q: Health data in a country town show that adults over 60 have a low rate of reported illness. A researcher then interviews residents about their health. What does the interview add that the data could not?
opts: How residents feel about their own health
How many residents are over 60
The rate of illness among those residents
Whether illness rates differ from other towns
b.why: Interviews can capture how people feel about their health, which rates cannot. The other three options are counts or comparisons, which epidemiology can already supply. The illness rate is tempting, but it is exactly what the data gave.
b.clue: Which option cannot be found by counting?

a.best: Why the rates differ between the regions

b.best: How residents feel about their own health

problems.detail: The stem says the report 'shows that diabetes rates are higher', but rates alone do not give absolute counts without population figures. 'How many people have diabetes in each region' is meant as something the report shows, yet a careful student could argue a rate report does not tell us this. Saying the report gives the number of cases and the rates would remove the doubt.

check.summary: Both questions are sound and the intended answers match the card. One small wording point: question a could say the report gives case numbers as well as rates, so the 'how many people' distractor is clearly something the report does tell us.
